references.text: Here too the Pharisees watched Jesus on a Sabbath to see if he would heal, showing the same pattern of hostile observation.
The scribes and chief priests kept watch on Jesus and sent spies to catch him in his words so they could accuse him—the same motive of finding grounds for accusation.
The parallel passage in Mark where they watched Jesus to see if he healed on the Sabbath, so they could accuse him.
The parallel passage in Matthew where the Pharisees asked Jesus whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, hoping to find something to accuse him of.
The scribes and Pharisees began to press Jesus hard and tried to provoke him into saying something they could use against him—the same hostile surveillance.
Earlier in the same chapter, the Pharisees criticized the disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, showing the ongoing conflict over Sabbath observance.
Also in John, the Pharisees accused Jesus of breaking the Sabbath after a healing, demonstrating the recurring pattern of Sabbath conflicts.
The wicked one watches the righteous and seeks to kill him—a prophetic picture of how the scribes and Pharisees watched Jesus to find grounds for accusation.
Jeremiah experienced friends watching him to find something to accuse him of, a parallel to how Jesus' opponents monitored him.
